**Murfreesboro, Tennessee**

According to a relative who spoke with CNN, a young mother and her baby daughter lost their lives when a tornado struck Murfreesboro, Tennessee on Friday. Family member Mark McClure identified the victims as Kori Bryant and her infant daughter Olivia, who were together at home when disaster struck. The mother's husband, John Bryant, was located roughly two houses down from their home, having suffered a collapsed lung along with fractures to his ribs and spine, McClure said. He was rushed to Vanderbilt University Hospital, where doctors plan to operate once his blood pressure levels out. McClure noted that John learned of his wife and daughter's deaths from his brother the previous day.

Donnie Smith, spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Emergency Management, explained that severe weather began developing around midday as a line of powerful thunderstorms moved through the state from the southwest. The tornado subsequently touched down in Murfreesboro—located in Rutherford County, roughly 30 miles from Nashville—just before 1:40 p.m.

Martha Tolbert, a spokeswoman for Middle Tennessee Medical Center, confirmed that three dozen individuals received treatment there for storm-related injuries. Smith added that rescue teams continued their search operations well into the evening hours.

**Mena, Arkansas**

Meanwhile, residents of Mena, Arkansas were left picking up the pieces after a separate tornado tore through their community Thursday night, killing three people and leaving over 100 homes damaged or demolished, according to state officials.

Captain Christopher Heathscott described the scene as resembling a "war zone," with National Guard troops conducting door-to-door searches for survivors. Approximately 50 soldiers assisted with maintaining security and distributing food supplies throughout the affected area.

Tommy Jackson of the state's emergency management department reported that the town, home to roughly 6,000 residents, suffered its worst damage on the western side before the storm cut through downtown and continued along Highway 71. Fellow department official James Reeves echoed the war-zone comparison, describing the destruction firsthand.

Reeves detailed extensive damage to critical infrastructure, including the local hospital, city hall, a middle school, several churches, the public library, a Masonic lodge, and the courthouse—which houses both the 911 dispatch center and a detention facility. He noted that the entire western portion of the city had lost both electrical power and gas service.

KTHV-TV correspondent Charles Crowson reported that two facilities within an industrial park had been leveled, with utility workers scrambling to contain a gas leak at the site. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd told Crowson that the county's detention center had become "uninhabitable" following the storm. The 18 inmates who had been housed there at the time were subsequently transferred to facilities in neighboring counties, he confirmed.

*Additional reporting contributed by CNN's Melissa Roberts and Dave Alsup.*

# Deadly Tornado Tears Through Murfreesboro, Tennessee, Leaving Trail of Destruction

**By CNN Staff**

*Murfreesboro, Tennessee* — A powerful tornado ripped through Murfreesboro overnight, killing at least six people and injuring dozens more as it flattened homes, businesses, and a section of downtown, officials said Thursday.

The National Weather Service confirmed the tornado touched down just after 11 p.m. Wednesday, carving a path of destruction roughly 15 miles long through Rutherford County. Preliminary assessments suggest the storm reached at least EF-3 strength, with wind speeds estimated between 140 and 165 mph.

## "It Sounded Like a Freight Train"

Residents described terrifying moments as the storm bore down with little warning.

"We had maybe two minutes to get to the basement," said Linda Carver, a longtime resident of the Blackman community, one of the hardest-hit areas. "By the time we came up, our neighbor's house was just gone. Slab foundation, nothing else."

Emergency sirens blared through the city as the tornado tore through residential neighborhoods near Blackman High School, damaging the school building and destroying dozens of homes in surrounding subdivisions.

## Victims Identified

Rutherford County officials on Thursday identified four of the six confirmed victims: Robert Ellison, 67; his wife, Diane Ellison, 64; James Whitfield, 41; and 9-year-old Mia Thornton, who died alongside her mother when their mobile home was destroyed. The identities of two additional victims were being withheld pending family notification.

Rutherford County Mayor Joe Carr called the losses "devastating" during a Thursday morning press conference.

"This community is in mourning, but it's also incredibly resilient," Carr said. "We will rebuild, and we will take care of one another, the way Murfreesboro always has."

## Dozens Injured, Hospitals Stretched Thin

Saint Thomas Rutherford Hospital reported treating more than 40 patients for storm-related injuries, ranging from lacerations and broken bones to more severe trauma. Hospital spokesperson Angela Reyes said at least eight patients remained in critical condition as of Thursday afternoon.

"Our emergency department teams worked through the night," Reyes said. "We're incredibly proud of how our staff responded under such difficult circumstances."

Middle Tennessee Medical Center, along with mutual aid units from surrounding counties, assisted in triaging patients as search-and-rescue crews combed through debris fields for survivors.

## Widespread Damage

Search-and-rescue teams, including Tennessee Task Force 1, worked block by block through the night using thermal imaging and K9 units to search collapsed structures. Rutherford County Emergency Management Agency Director Andy Farley said more than 200 homes were destroyed or severely damaged, with total losses expected to climb once assessments are complete.

Middle Tennessee State University, located in Murfreesboro, canceled classes for the remainder of the week after several campus buildings sustained roof damage and downed power lines closed off entrances.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee declared a state of emergency for Rutherford County on Thursday, activating the Tennessee National Guard to assist with cleanup and security in affected neighborhoods.

"Our hearts are with the families who lost loved ones and everyone whose homes were destroyed," Lee said in a statement. "The state stands ready to support Murfreesboro every step of the way."

## Community Response

Volunteers began arriving at makeshift relief centers Thursday morning, dropping off water, clothing, and supplies. The American Red Cross opened two shelters at local churches to house displaced families.

"We've had people show up we don't even know, just wanting to help clear debris," said Pastor Michael Simmons of First Baptist Church, one of the shelter sites. "That's Murfreesboro. That's Tennessee."

Officials urged residents to avoid storm-damaged areas to allow search-and-rescue operations to continue and to prevent injuries from downed power lines and unstable structures.

The National Weather Service warned that additional severe weather could move through the region by the weekend, urging residents to remain vigilant as recovery efforts continue.

"This was an extremely fast-moving and violent system," said a NWS meteorologist based in Memphis. "We're still conducting damage surveys, but early indications point to long-track tornadoes that stayed on the ground for extended periods, which explains the scope of destruction we're seeing."

## Casualties and Hospital Response

Officials have confirmed at least seven fatalities across both states, with dozens more individuals hospitalized in critical or serious condition. Numbers are expected to rise as search efforts continue in the hardest-hit areas.

Regional hospitals activated mass casualty protocols within the first hour of the storms making landfall. Baptist Memorial Hospital and several rural medical centers in northeast Arkansas reported surges of trauma patients, with some facilities forced to divert non-emergency patients to neighboring counties due to capacity strain.

"We saw everything from lacerations and broken bones to severe crush injuries," said a hospital spokesperson in Jackson, Tennessee. "Our emergency department teams worked through the night, and additional staff were called in from off-duty rotations to manage the volume of patients."

Several hospitals in the affected zones sustained structural damage themselves, including a regional medical center in Arkansas that reported partial roof failure in one wing, forcing evacuation of patients to unaffected areas of the building. Generators kept critical care units operational after power grids failed across the region.

## Search-and-Rescue Operations

Search-and-rescue teams, including local fire departments, state emergency management personnel, and National Guard units, have been deployed to the most severely affected communities. Canine search units and drone teams equipped with thermal imaging have been brought in to assist in locating survivors trapped beneath debris.

"Our priority right now is life safety," said an emergency management official overseeing operations in one of the hardest-hit Tennessee counties. "We're conducting primary and secondary searches of every structure in the damage path. Crews are working block by block."

Rescue crews reported pulling multiple survivors from collapsed homes and mobile home communities, which sustained some of the most catastrophic damage. Officials urged residents in affected areas to avoid downed power lines and unstable structures while search operations continue.

## Infrastructure Damage

The destruction to infrastructure across both states has been extensive. Utility companies report tens of thousands of customers without power, with some transmission lines completely destroyed and requiring full rebuilding rather than repair. Cell service has been intermittent in several counties due to damaged communications towers, complicating both rescue coordination and efforts by residents to reach loved ones.

Multiple roadways remain impassable due to fallen trees, debris, and in some cases, complete pavement destruction from the tornadoes' path. State transportation departments have closed sections of highway in both states, rerouting traffic as crews work to clear debris.

Entire neighborhoods have been leveled, with local officials comparing the damage to previous historic outbreaks in the region. Schools, churches, and small businesses in the storms' path were reported destroyed or severely damaged, and at least two water treatment facilities suffered damage, prompting boil-water advisories for affected communities.

## Response and Relief Efforts

Governors in both Tennessee and Arkansas have declared states of emergency, freeing up state resources and paving the way for federal disaster assistance requests. The American Red Cross has opened emergency shelters in several communities, and local churches and civic organizations have mobilized to provide food, water, and temporary housing for displaced residents.

Officials are asking residents to avoid affected areas unless necessary to allow emergency crews unimpeded access, and are directing those seeking information on missing loved ones to contact designated hotlines set up by local emergency management agencies.

As daylight breaks over the affected regions, officials caution that damage assessments are still in early stages, and the full scope of the tragedy may not be known for several days. Additional severe weather remains possible later this week, according to forecasters, prompting concern among officials already stretched thin by recovery operations.
